title_en: Wang Huiwen v. Zhuhai Xinguang Futures Brokerage Co., Ltd. — dispute over futures agency
keywords_en: civil; dispute over futures agency contract; first instance; intermediate people's court; Guangdong Province; natural person; legal person; contract law; whether a futures brokerage company entered the market for trading according to client's instructions; allocation of burden of proof; in favor of plaintiff; futures agency; unauthorized offset; bucket trading; forced liquidation; margin loss; good faith; contract dispute; guarantee; futures agency dispute of a brokerage limited company
full_text_en:
Wang Huiwen v. Zhuhai Xinguang Futures Brokerage Co., Ltd.

——Dispute over futures agency contract

Plaintiff: Wang Huiwen, male, 32 years old, residing at Room 102, Building 5, Lianhua Mountain, Jida, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province.

Agent ad litem: Li Bailiang, lawyer of Yian Law Firm, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province.

Defendant: Zhuhai Xinguang Futures Brokerage Co., Ltd., Guangdong Province.

Legal representative: Xu Chengyong, manager.

Agent ad litem: Wang Weidong and Fan Huijun, lawyers of Hongyuan Law Firm, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province.

The plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, filed a lawsuit with the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province against the defendant, Zhuhai Xinguang Futures Brokerage Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xinguang Company), concerning a dispute over a futures agency contract.

The plaintiff alleged: The plaintiff entrusted the defendant to act as agent for futures business. The defendant failed to enter the market in accordance with the plaintiff's instructions, engaged in off-exchange offsetting and betting against clients, thereby seriously infringing upon the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests. The plaintiff requested the court to order the defendant to compensate the plaintiff for losses of margin in the amount of RMB 1,186,000, interest of RMB 10,000, and commission losses of RMB 54,000.

The defendant did not file a defense.

The Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court ascertained through trial:

The defendant, Xinguang Company, had the business scope of acting as agent for domestic futures, but was not a member of the Shanghai Commodity Exchange (hereinafter referred to as the SCE). Through signing a "Futures Trading Entrusted Agency Contract" with Shanghai Zhongqi Futures Brokerage Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongqi Company), a member of the SCE, Xinguang Company entrusted Zhongqi Company to act as its agent for futures trading on the SCE.

On September 13, 1995, the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, and the defendant, Xinguang Company, entered into a "Futures Business Entrusted Agency Agreement." It was agreed that after Wang Huiwen deposited an initial margin of RMB 500,000, Xinguang Company would act as his agent for domestic or international futures, options, and spot trading of commodities and financial instruments; Xinguang Company had the right to modify margin requirements and collect agency fees. Wang Huiwen also signed documents including an account opening application, a risk disclosure statement, a client seal authorization letter, and a broker authorization letter, and deposited a margin of RMB 500,000 on the same day.

Subsequently, the defendant, Xinguang Company, acted as agent for the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, in several domestic commodity futures transactions involving plywood, coffee, and soybean meal. During the trading period, Wang Huiwen also made additional margin deposits multiple times. By October 16, 1995, the funds in Wang Huiwen's account with Xinguang Company amounted to RMB 1,260,973.

From October 16 to 24, 1995, the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, gave oral instructions to the defendant, Xinguang Company, to sell short 1,800 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood by opening positions. With respect to Wang Huiwen's instructions, Xinguang Company indicated on the "Transaction Record Slips" submitted to Wang Huiwen that all instructions had been fully executed and transactions had been concluded, with the transaction prices and volumes consistent with Wang Huiwen's instructions. At that time, Wang Huiwen believed that his trading account held open positions of 1,800 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood. On October 31, Xinguang Company notified Wang Huiwen that, due to a position limit notice issued by the SCE regarding Shanghai 95.11 plywood, Xinguang Company had forcibly liquidated 1,300 of Wang Huiwen's 1,800 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood. According to the "Transaction Record Slips" provided by Xinguang Company after the liquidation, the liquidation price was RMB 48.60 per lot, resulting in a loss of RMB 920,000 for Wang Huiwen. From November 1 to 8, Wang Huiwen issued instructions to Xinguang Company to close the remaining 500 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood. According to the "Transaction Record Slips" provided by Xinguang Company, Wang Huiwen suffered a total loss of RMB 1,186,000 from these two liquidations, and Xinguang Company charged commissions of RMB 54,000 for the two liquidations.

In January 1996, the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, learned that after entering the delivery month, some other clients still held up to 200 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood futures. This raised doubts about the authenticity and legality of the position limit notice and the forced liquidation claimed by Xinguang Company, so he requested an inquiry. Xinguang Company provided Wang Huiwen with several "Profit and Loss Statements for Closed Position Contracts" prepared by Shanghai Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone Development Co., Ltd. and issued to Xinguang Company. Wang Huiwen believed that the figures on these statements showed signs of alteration and could not prove that they were the result of his instructions, and therefore raised objections. At that time, Xinguang Company stated that the profit and loss statements provided to Wang Huiwen were erroneous and that Wang Huiwen's entrusted instructions were actually placed by Zhongqi Company. Xinguang Company then provided Wang Huiwen with several "Transaction Result Notices" issued by Zhongqi Company. Wang Huiwen still believed that these notices could not prove that they were the result of executing his instructions, and thus filed the lawsuit.

During the litigation, the defendant, Xinguang Company, submitted three types of evidence to the court to prove that it had executed the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen's instructions: first, seven pages of "Transaction Result Notices" issued by Zhongqi Company to Xinguang Company, the contents of which were all handwritten; second, nine pages of "Daily Transaction Lists for Members" issued by the SCE to Zhongqi Company, with Xinguang Company pointing out that one page contained records of executing Wang Huiwen's instructions; and third, the "Transaction Record Slips" provided by Xinguang Company to Wang Huiwen. Wang Huiwen also submitted to the court three types of materials prepared by the SCE for other clients: first, "Daily Transaction Lists for Members," which were consistent with the second type of evidence submitted by Xinguang Company; second, "Profit and Loss Statements for Open Position Contracts"; and third, "Daily Receipts and Payments Settlement Statements for Members." Xinguang Company could not provide the latter two types of evidence submitted by Wang Huiwen. Upon the court's request for evidence from Zhongqi Company, Zhongqi Company also could not submit these two types of evidence to the court.

Upon comparing the three types of evidence submitted by the defendant, Xinguang Company, the following issues were identified:

First, inconsistency in the number of opened positions. The "Transaction Record Slips" reflected that the defendant, Xinguang Company, opened 1,800 lots on behalf of the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, whereas the "Transaction Result Notices" and the "Daily Transaction Lists for Members" both reflected 1,650 lots, a difference of 150 lots. Xinguang Company later admitted during the litigation that only 1,650 lots were actually transacted. However, prior to the litigation, Wang Huiwen had always believed that 1,800 lots had been opened and that the corresponding liquidation was also for 1,800 lots.

Second, inconsistency in client codes between the opening and forced liquidation of positions. For 1,100 lots, there were four client codes at the time of opening: 13020034, 13040048, 13020020, and 13020098; at the time of liquidation, there were only two client codes: 13020028 and 13020098. For another 400 lots, the client codes at the time of opening were 13010015 and 13020098, while the client codes at the time of liquidation were 13020034 and 13020169.

Third, inconsistency in prices. The defendant, Xinguang Company, claimed that all transactions were executed at the prices instructed by the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen. However, according to the "Transaction Result Notices" issued by Zhongqi Company to Xinguang Company and the "Daily Transaction Lists for Members" issued by the SCE to Zhongqi Company, most transaction prices did not match the prices communicated to Wang Huiwen by Xinguang Company. For example, for 400 lots sold short, Xinguang Company told Wang Huiwen that the transaction was concluded at RMB 45.60, but the records of Zhongqi Company and the SCE showed a transaction price of RMB 45.50, which was RMB 0.10 lower than the instructed price; for 100 lots sold short, Xinguang Company told Wang Huiwen that the transaction was concluded at RMB 45.60, but the records of Zhongqi Company and the SCE showed a transaction price of RMB 45.70, which was RMB 0.10 higher than the instructed price. In terms of liquidation, for 100 lots, Xinguang Company claimed that the transaction was concluded at RMB 49.10 and settled with Wang Huiwen, but the records of Zhongqi Company and the SCE showed a transaction price of RMB 49.20, which was RMB 0.10 higher than the instructed price. Xinguang Company never informed Wang Huiwen of these discrepancies in transaction prices.

Fourth, reversed direction of position orders. For example, the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, instructed the opening of 300 lots on October 17, 100 lots on October 23, and 200 lots on October 24. According to the SCE records, these position orders were not recorded as openings but as closings. The defendant, Xinguang Company, never informed Wang Huiwen of the reversed direction of the position orders.

The Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court held at first instance:

The futures business entrusted agency agreement signed between the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen, and the defendant, Xinguang Company, constitutes a valid civil act and shall be protected by law. In futures trading, a futures brokerage firm and its client form a commission agency relationship. The broker, in its own name, buys and sells futures on behalf of the client according to the client's instructions and bears legal liability for acts that violate the client's instructions and futures trading operational rules. Due to the special nature of this industry, clients generally can only understand the true situation of their transactions through the broker. Therefore, when a client doubts whether the broker has entered the market for trading according to the instructions, the broker shall bear the burden of proof; if the broker fails to provide corresponding evidence, it shall be determined that the broker did not enter the market for trading. The principle "he who asserts must prove" does not apply here. Wang Huiwen alleged that Xinguang Company did not enter the market for trading according to his instructions and engaged in off-exchange offsetting and betting against clients. Xinguang Company bears the burden of proof for this.

The defendant, Xinguang Company, has already admitted during the litigation that it failed to open positions for 150 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood futures as instructed by the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen. The court accepts this admission during litigation. The three types of evidence submitted by Xinguang Company to prove that the remaining 1,650 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood futures had been entered into the market for trading not only had problems such as inconsistency in the number of opened positions, mismatched client codes, inconsistency in prices, and reversed direction of position orders, but also included violations of the "SCE Trading Rules," such as failure to execute client limit orders at the specified price or better, and failure to adhere to the principles of member application, one account per client code, and exclusive use of each client code. Due to the existence of these problems, Xinguang Company could only point out from the evidence it submitted which records were based on Wang Huiwen's instructions for market entry. The court could not objectively analyze these records as being the result of Wang Huiwen's instructions. The evidence submitted by Xinguang Company could not prove that the company had executed Wang Huiwen's instructions. It shall be presumed that Xinguang Company did not enter the market for trading the 1,650 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood futures bought and sold by Wang Huiwen. Under these circumstances, Xinguang Company had no lawful basis to deduct from Wang Huiwen's futures trading margin account the trading loss of RMB 1,186,000 and the commission of RMB 54,000 for these 1,800 lots of Shanghai 95.11 plywood futures. Xinguang Company shall, in accordance with Article 61 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, return these two sums to Wang Huiwen and compensate for the corresponding interest losses. Accordingly, the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on March 28, 1997:

The defendant, Xinguang Company, shall, within ten days from the date this judgment takes legal effect, return RMB 1,240,000 and the interest thereon to the plaintiff, Wang Huiwen. In case of late payment, it shall be handled in accordance with Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The court acceptance fee for the first instance, RMB 16,710, shall be borne by Xinguang Company.

The defendant, Xinguang Company, refused to accept the judgment of the first instance and appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court. The grounds for appeal were: The evidence submitted by the appellant to the court of first instance has already proved that the instructions of the appellee, Wang Huiwen, had entered the trading market. The problems with the evidence were caused by the "first-in, first-out" and mixed position operation methods commonly adopted by most domestic first-tier and second-tier agency companies for convenience and speed in trading and to save margin, which are common and normal phenomena. Moreover, the instructions filled out by Wang Huiwen were not limit orders, so there was no issue of inconsistency between the transaction price and the limit order price. The court of first instance inferred from these problems that the appellant did not enter the market for trading according to Wang Huiwen's instructions. This reasoning was untenable. The appellant requested the judgment be changed to dismiss Wang Huiwen's claims.

After trial, the Guangdong High People's Court held that: This case involves a domestic commodity futures dispute. The parties involved in the futures trading complied with legal requirements. The dispute centered on whether the market entry trading conduct of the futures brokerage company existed and was lawful and valid. The court of first instance had already pointed out that the evidence submitted by the appellant, Xinguang Company, contained a series of defects. These defects fully demonstrated that Xinguang Company not only failed to operate in accordance with the SCE rules, but also, after the dispute arose, could not submit valid evidence to prove that it had entered the market for trading according to the instructions of the appellee, Wang Huiwen. The court of first instance was correct in determining that Xinguang Company did not enter the market for trading according to Wang Huiwen's instructions and in ordering Xinguang Company to bear the civil liability of returning the margin and compensating for interest losses. The final trading of futures occurs on the SCE, and whether trading conduct is standardized shall be assessed according to the SCE rules. The appellant, Xinguang Company's argument that "first-in, first-out" and mixed position operations and other irregular practices are common and normal phenomena in the industry cannot constitute a ground for exemption from liability. Regarding the appellant's argument that Wang Huiwen's instructions were not limit orders, this is inconsistent with the facts, and the determination that there was no market entry was not based solely on the presence or absence of a limit order. This ground of appeal is also untenable. The judgment of the first instance had clear factual findings, correct application of law, and appropriate handling, and should be affirmed. Accordingly, the Guangdong High People's Court, in accordance with Article 153(1)(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on March 10, 1998: Appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.
